newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris airshow highlights Europe space agency woes.
newsitem.headline: Paris airshow highlights Europe space agency woes.

text.p: The European Space Agency (ESA) faces a bumpy road ahead due to tight budgets, infighting and lingering bitterness over a disastrous rocket explosion last year, its new chief said on Wednesday.

"The European financial situation is very difficult for the Agency and for the member states...We must obtain the same results with less money. This will not be easy, but the industry has shown that it is entirely possible," said Antony Rodota, incoming ESA director.

Rodota, in an interview at the Paris airshow, defended large expenditures on ESA as long-term investments in the interests of Europe but acknowledged that the agency would have to adapt to deal with new financial strictures.
"Space will be playing a more and more important role not only in traditional fields of satellites, space stations and science but also in its (pratical) applications," he said.

"To obtain our objectives, we must change. It isnt possible that the Agency achieves its objective alone. It must have public opinion behind it. The public must understand that money used for space is not just spent but invested," Rodota said.

Rodota, an Italian, is slated to take over the 14 member-nation ESA on July 1. The Agency coordinates Europe's space activities from scientific and international collaboration to the Ariane-5 heavy lift satellite launcher.
The agency's marquis programme, its heavy satellite launchers, represent the largest share of ESAs budget and 25 percent of 1997's $2.2 billion budget was spent on the ten-year, $9 billion programme.

But that project is in serious difficulty after the spectacular failure last year of the first Ariane-5 rocket, which blew up 37 seconds after lift-off from the ESA launch centre in Kourou, French Guiana due to faulty software in the rocket's guidance system.

The rocket was designed to keep Europe in the lead in launching heavy satellites well into the next century and eventually, to lead to a European-manned rocket. Its failure has cast a cloud over ESA's ability to remain the leader in the lucrative heavy launch vehicle field and delayed the commercial entry of Ariane-5, set for early 1997, for at least a year.
A second flight is scheduled for late September, but officials indicated further delays were likely.
"We will do everything possible to make (the flight) a success and will delay the launch if necessary," said Fredrik Engstrom, ESA director of launchers.
Arianespace, which has commercial responsibility for ESA's satellite launch activities, was the uncontested leader in the heavy satellite launch market from the mid 1980's.
But now, rival International Launch Service's (ILS), a joint venture between U.S. aerospace giant Lockheed Martin and Russian and Ukrainian firms, says it has just as much market share.

Another potential Arianespace problem comes from a bitter battle to replace retiring Charles Bigot for the top job. The fight took a twist this week as the new Socialist-led government delayed appointing outgoing ESA head Jean-Marie Luton.
Luton was the favourite for Arianespace's top job before Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin came to power earlier this month in an upset victory in a parliamentary election.
The former, conservative French government all but eliminated Bigot's handpicked successor as a candidate in April.
Bigot was reported furious at the turn of events and was not present at the show, which is normally a showcase for his company's image.
The French government controls Arianespace with its 55-percent share through state-owned companies and organisations. The French Space Agency (CNES) alone holds 33 percent.
